section.title: Macedonia, Troas, and the Farewell at Miletus
section.sectionRationale: The third missionary journey draws to a close. Paul revisits the churches of Macedonia and Greece, raises Eutychus at Troas on the Lord's Day, and, sailing past Ephesus to make Jerusalem by Pentecost, summons the Ephesian elders to Miletus for a farewell that is really a charge: guard the flock God bought with His own blood.
section.thesis: As Paul sets his face for Jerusalem and chains, he hands the churches over to God and to the word of His grace, entrusting the flock to elders whom the Spirit has made overseers to shepherd the church that Christ purchased with His own blood.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the road through Macedonia and Greece; Eutychus raised at Troas; the coasting voyage to Miletus; Paul's example and his Spirit-driven course to Jerusalem; the charge to guard the flock; and the tearful parting on the shore.

units.label: Through Macedonia and Greece
units.note: revisiting the churches, evading a plot

verses.text: When the uproar had ended, Paul sent for the disciples. And after encouraging them, he said goodbye to them and left for Macedonia.
After traveling through that area and speaking many words of encouragement, he arrived in Greece,
where he stayed three months. And when the Jews formed a plot against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia.
Paul was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia.
These men went on ahead and waited for us in Troas.
And after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi, and five days later we rejoined them in Troas, where we stayed seven days.

units.label: Eutychus raised at Troas
units.note: the first day of the week, life restored

verses.text: On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Since Paul was ready to leave the next day, he talked to them and kept on speaking until midnight.
Now there were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.
And a certain young man named Eutychus, seated in the window, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on. When he was sound asleep, he fell from the third story and was picked up dead.
But Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and embraced him. “Do not be alarmed!” he said. “He is still alive!”
Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, and ate. And after speaking until daybreak, he departed.
And the people were greatly relieved to take the boy home alive.

units.label: The coasting voyage to Miletus
units.note: hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost

verses.text: We went on ahead to the ship and sailed to Assos, where we were to take Paul aboard. He had arranged this because he was going there on foot.
And when he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene.
Sailing on from there, we arrived the next day opposite Chios. The day after that we arrived at Samos, and on the following day we came to Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus to avoid spending time in the province of Asia, because he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus, Paul sent to Ephesus for the {{presbyteros|elders}} of the church.

units.label: Paul's example and his course to Jerusalem
units.note: the whole will of God, compelled by the Spirit

verses.text: When they came to him, he said, “You know how I lived the whole time I was with you, from the first day I arrived in the province of Asia.
I served the Lord with great humility and with tears, especially in the trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews.
I did not shrink back from declaring anything that was helpful to you as I taught you publicly and from house to house,
testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now, compelled by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there.
I only know that in town after town the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and afflictions await me.
But I consider my life of no value to me, if only I may finish my course and complete the ministry I have received from the Lord Jesus, the ministry of testifying to the good news of God’s grace.
Now I know that none of you among whom I have preached the kingdom will see my face again.
Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all men.
For I did not shrink back from declaring to you the whole will of God.

units.label: Guard the flock God bought
units.note: the church purchased with His own blood

verses.text: Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you {{episkopos|overseers}}. {{poimaino|Be shepherds}} of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.
I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock.
Even from your own number, men will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them.
Therefore be alert and remember that for three years I never stopped warning each of you night and day with tears.
And now I commit you to God and to the word of His {{charis|grace}}, which can build you up and give you an inheritance among all who are sanctified.
I have not coveted anyone’s silver or gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs and those of my companions.
In everything, I showed you that by this kind of hard work we must help the weak, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus Himself: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

units.label: The tearful farewell
units.note: kneeling to pray on the shore

verses.text: When Paul had said this, he knelt down with all of them and prayed.
They all wept openly as they embraced Paul and kissed him.
They were especially grieved by his statement that they would never see his face again. Then they accompanied him to the ship.

presbyteros.gloss: Elder; a mature, appointed leader in the church. Paul sends to Ephesus for the presbyteroi, and in the same speech calls these very men episkopoi, overseers, and charges them to shepherd, so the three terms describe one office seen from different angles.

episkopos.gloss: Overseer, guardian, one who watches over. The Holy Spirit, not merely the church, has made the elders overseers; their authority is a stewardship received from God to guard His people against wolves and distortion.

poimaino.gloss: To shepherd, tend, and feed a flock. The word gives us pastor. The elders are to do for the church what a shepherd does for sheep: feed, protect, and lead, under Christ the Chief Shepherd who owns the flock.

charis.gloss: Grace, undeserved favor. Paul commits the elders not to himself but to God and to the word of His grace, the gospel message that has power to build them up and secure their inheritance among the sanctified.

basic.context: Paul is finishing his third journey. He revisits the churches of Macedonia and Greece, and on the way back stops at Troas, where a young man named Eutychus falls to his death from a window during a long night sermon and Paul restores him alive. Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul sails past Ephesus but calls its elders to meet him at Miletus for a farewell speech, the one full address to Christians in Acts. He is going to chains, and he wants the shepherds ready.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative, but the Miletus speech is teaching within the narrative, the closest thing in Acts to a pastoral letter spoken aloud. Read it as Paul's charge to church leaders in every age: watch yourselves and the flock, expect opposition from without and from within, and rest the church on God and the word of His grace rather than on any human leader.
basic.originalLanguages: One office is named three ways. Paul sends for the presbyteroi, elders, then says the Spirit made them episkopoi, overseers, and tells them to poimainein, to shepherd. Elder, overseer, and pastor are the same men and the same office. He commits them to the word of God's charis, His grace, which alone can build them up.
basic.typology: Paul the departing shepherd who warns of wolves and commends the flock to God stands in a long line: Moses, Joshua, and Samuel all gave farewell charges to God's people. Above them all stands Christ the Good Shepherd, who unlike Paul does not merely warn of danger but lays down His life for the sheep and buys them with His own blood.
basic.christ: The center of the speech is verse 28: the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood. The flock is precious because of the price paid for it, the blood of Christ. Every faithful pastor since serves a people bought at that cost. Paul's own readiness to face chains and death for the ministry mirrors the self-giving of the Lord Jesus he preaches.
basic.god: God the Holy Spirit compels Paul toward Jerusalem, warns him of chains, and appoints the elders as overseers. God the Father owns the church and purchases it. Paul entrusts everything to God and to the word of His grace, confident that God, not Paul, keeps the church.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 5:1-4 gives the same charge, elders shepherding the flock under the Chief Shepherd. Ephesians 4:11 lists pastors and teachers as Christ's gift. John 10 shows the Good Shepherd laying down His life. Ezekiel 34 warns of false shepherds who fail the flock God will Himself come to save.
basic.oneStory: As the gospel presses on from Jerusalem toward Rome, Paul makes sure the churches he planted will stand after he is gone. He hands them to God and to the word of grace and to shepherds who must guard the blood-bought flock. The mission outlives the missionary because the church belongs to Christ, who purchased it and keeps it.

context.literary:
The chapter has two halves joined by a journey. The first half is a travel report with one vivid scene at Troas, the raising of Eutychus (20:7-12). The second half is the Miletus address (20:18-35), the only speech in Acts delivered to Christians, and it is shaped with unusual care. Paul begins by looking back (20:18-21), turns to the present and the road ahead (20:22-27), gives the charge itself (20:28-31), and ends by commending the elders to God and offering his own conduct as an example (20:32-35). The two halves of the speech are tied by an inclusio. In verse 20 he says he did not 'shrink back' from declaring what was helpful, and in verse 27 he says he did not 'shrink back' from declaring the whole will of God. Tears also frame it, in verses 19 and 31, and so does the phrase 'I know' in verses 25 and 29.

The voice of the passage is closer to Paul's letters than any other speech Luke gives him. Humility, tears, testifying, grace, inheritance and sanctification are all vocabulary of his epistles. Luke is also present as an eyewitness here, since the 'we' reappears in verses 5 and 6 and runs on through the voyage. The farewell has the genre feel of a testament. Moses (Deuteronomy 31 to 33), Joshua (Joshua 23 and 24) and Samuel (1 Samuel 12) all addressed Israel at the end of their service in similar steps: a review of faithful service, a warning, a handing over. Luke wants readers to hear Paul in that line.

The placement matters too. The scene at Troas, in which a young man dies and is given back, comes just before a speech in which Paul talks of going to chains and probable death. The tale of the lamps and the window is not a digression. It is a small picture of resurrection at the start of a long road toward suffering.
context.historical:
Paul has spent three months in Greece, almost certainly in Corinth, and during that time wrote his letter to the Romans, telling them he was on his way to Jerusalem with the collection from Macedonia and Achaia (Romans 15:25-27). A plot by Jews as he was about to sail for Syria forced him to change plans and go back through Macedonia (20:3). The seven men who travel with him in verse 4 come from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe and Asia, and they are very probably the delegates carrying the churches' gifts. That detail matters because it shows the whole company is travelling to Jerusalem for an act of love and not for an adventure.

The first day of the week at Troas is one of the earliest glimpses of Christian practice. The believers gather to break bread, and Paul speaks until midnight because he will leave the next day. The upper room was lit by many lamps, a note that fits the stuffy air and the sleepiness of a young man who had perhaps worked all day. Windows in such rooms were open frames, not glass, so a boy seated in one could fall three storeys.

Miletus was a port city some distance south of Ephesus, and Paul's refusal to go to Ephesus was prudent, because a visit to a church he knew so well would have used up days he did not have if he were to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, the feast of Shavuot, as verse 16 says. He sends for the elders instead. The word elders points to the way Jewish and early Christian communities were governed, by a plurality of older and proved men, not by a single ruler. The speech is also a moment of real danger in the church's history, because the false teaching Paul predicts did arrive in Asia, as 1 Timothy 1:3-7 and 2 Timothy 1:15 show.
context.canonical:
The Miletus address is the New Testament's fullest picture of what a church leader is. Its themes recur in the Pastoral Epistles. Titus 1:5-7 moves in a single paragraph from appointing 'elders' to describing the 'overseer', as if the words were interchangeable. 1 Timothy 3:1-7 gives the character list for an overseer, and 1 Peter 5:1-4 reproduces nearly all of Paul's charge: elders are to shepherd God's flock, not by compulsion or for gain, but as examples, answering to the Chief Shepherd. When Hebrews 13:17 says leaders keep watch over souls as those who must give an account, it names the weight Paul has just put on the elders.

Behind all of that stands the Old Testament picture of God's shepherds. Ezekiel 34 condemns the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves and not the flock, and promises that the LORD Himself will search for His sheep. Ezekiel 33:1-9 describes the watchman who must warn or be held accountable for the blood of those who perish, and Paul's claim in verse 26 that he is innocent of the blood of all men plainly echoes it. The BSB footnote points to the same passage. David the shepherd king, Moses and the prophets all stand in the background.

The speech is also a hinge in the book's story of the church. After this the narrative follows Paul to Jerusalem and into prison. The churches he planted will have to stand on their own, which is why the final verses are handed to God and to the word of His grace. Jesus Himself used the wolf in John 10:12 and Matthew 7:15, and Revelation 2:2 shows the Ephesian church later testing and exposing those who falsely claimed to be apostles, evidence that the elders listened.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke gives Paul's farewell this much room because the church he is describing in the second half of Acts will have to live without apostles. Paul does not hand over a rulebook or a system of ranks. He hands over three things: his own example, a warning, and a commendation to God. The example is humility, tears, public and private teaching, hard work with his own hands, and willingness to suffer. The warning is that wolves will come from outside and men will rise up from within who twist the truth in order to gather followers. The commendation is to God and to the word of His grace, which can build up and give an inheritance.

Luke wants Gentile readers a generation later, who are living with those very dangers, to hear that their own leaders were told this in advance and that the foundation is intended to hold. He also wants them to see what true leadership costs. The elders are not asked to be impressive. They are asked to watch, to feed, and to remember a man who wept over them for three years night and day.

There is a personal edge too. Paul does not claim to know what will happen in Jerusalem apart from the Spirit's warnings, and he does not hide that he expects chains. The hearers are meant to learn that a leader can be certain of his calling and uncertain about his future at once, and that this is a place of trust rather than anxiety.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Luke narrates a good deal here that is purely descriptive: the route, the delegates, the ship, the lamps, the fall of Eutychus. The first day gathering at Troas is described, not legislated; Luke does not say that all Christians must meet on Sundays or that every sermon should run to midnight, and he lightly lets us see that a long talk can send a listener to sleep. The raising of Eutychus is also an event, not a promise that Christian worship will always be marked by such things.\n\nThe charge in verses 28 to 35 is another matter. It is spoken to leaders in the second person with imperatives: keep watch, be shepherds, be alert, remember. These carry forward to every generation of elders, not because they are Paul's habits but because the reasons he gives never expire: the Spirit appointed overseers, the church was bought with blood, wolves come, and the word of grace builds up. The quoted saying of Jesus, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive', is a command shape for all believers, though it appears in no Gospel. Paul's refusal to take money from them is described as his own practice, an example to the weak, and in other places he teaches that those who preach have a right to support, 1 Corinthians 9:14. The pattern is not a rule that every pastor must be self-supporting.

debates.question: Are elder, overseer, and pastor three offices or one?

views.label: One office, three terms
views.case: In this one speech Paul calls the same men elders, says the Spirit made them overseers, and commands them to shepherd. Titus 1:5-7 likewise moves from elder to overseer for the same person, and 1 Peter 5:1-2 has elders exercising oversight and shepherding. The strongest case is that the words describe one office by its dignity, its duty of oversight, and its shepherd care.

views.label: Distinct offices or ranks
views.case: Later church history distinguished bishop, presbyter, and pastor into separate orders, and some read a developing hierarchy already implied. The strongest case points to the practical need for order and to the singular the overseer in the Pastorals as a recognized position.

debates.bearing: If the terms name one office, then every faithful pastor is an elder charged to oversee and shepherd, accountable to guard the flock; the passage levels ministry under Christ the Chief Shepherd rather than building a ladder of ranks.

debates.question: What does 'His own blood' mean in verse 28?

views.label: The blood of God Himself, because the Son is God
views.case: The sentence says the church of God was purchased with His own blood. Read straightforwardly, the one who bought the church is God, and the blood is His. Because Jesus is God made flesh, what He shed can be called God's own blood, just as one can say that God was born in Bethlehem or died on the cross. The strongest case is that the plain reading honours the unity of the Son's person and the weight of Paul's words.

views.label: The blood of His Own, meaning His own Son
views.case: The BSB footnote notes the option 'with the blood of His own Son'. The Greek can be taken as 'the blood of His Own', and Paul elsewhere calls Jesus God's own Son (Romans 8:32). On this reading Paul avoids saying that the divine nature bled, and keeps the thought that the Father paid with the One who was His own. The strongest case is the grammar and the usual caution about attributing blood to God as such.

views.label: A textual question, whether the church is the church of God or of the Lord
views.case: Some manuscripts read 'church of the Lord' instead of 'church of God', as the footnote records, and a few combine them. If 'the Lord' is read, the Lord is Christ and the problem seems to ease, though the phrase 'His own blood' still points to the owner of the church. The strongest case is simply that the reading 'of God' is the better attested and the harder one, the kind a scribe would be tempted to soften.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree on what matters: the flock was bought at the highest price, and the Father and the Son are united in that purchase. That is why a shepherd who neglects the sheep is dealing with something God Himself paid for.

debates.question: Was Eutychus dead, or only knocked senseless?

views.label: He was dead and was raised
views.case: Luke says he was picked up dead, the word nekros used elsewhere of corpses, and he sets the scene beside the stories of Elijah, who stretched himself over a boy (1 Kings 17:21-22), and Elisha (2 Kings 4:34-35). The strongest case is that Luke, who writes carefully, presents this as a resurrection and not as a lucky escape.

views.label: He was unconscious and Paul reassured the crowd
views.case: Paul's words, 'Do not be alarmed, he is still alive', literally 'his life is in him', could mean that the boy had not in fact died. The strongest case is that Paul's statement can be read as a diagnosis, and Luke's phrase 'picked up dead' may describe how the crowd saw it, not the medical fact.

debates.bearing: On either reading the story shows God's gentle power in the middle of a long sermon and a hard road. It does not turn on the medical question, but the first reading best fits the way Luke tells it and the Old Testament pattern he echoes.

study.originalLanguages:
The central verse, 28, repays slow reading. Paul tells the elders to 'keep watch' over themselves and the flock. The Greek verb prosecho means to turn the mind toward something, to give it heed, and Paul puts himself first in the list: the shepherd must look at his own life before he looks at the sheep. The word for 'flock' here is poimnion, and the word for 'overseers' is episkopoi, which gives us the word bishop but in this context simply means those who watch over a thing. The verb 'be shepherds' is poimaino, the same verb Jesus uses when He tells Peter to tend His sheep, John 21:16. One verse thus holds three words for the same work: oversight, shepherding, and watchfulness.

The phrase 'purchased with His own blood' uses the verb peripoieomai, to acquire for oneself, a word that carries the idea of securing something as a possession. The related noun appears in 1 Peter 2:9, where the church is 'a people for God's own possession', and in Ephesians 1:14, where believers are God's possession. Greek Isaiah 43:21 uses the same verb for the people God formed for Himself. Paul is saying that the church is God's acquired treasure.

In verse 24 the 'course' is dromos, a running track or a race, and Paul's wish to 'finish' it is the same picture he uses at the end of his life, 2 Timothy 4:7. He calls his work a diakonia, a service, and what he does is diamartyromai, to testify solemnly, as a witness under oath. The word turns up in verses 21 and 24 and sums up what he does: he testifies to repentance and faith and to the gospel of grace.

In verse 32 'commit' translates paratithemai, to place alongside for safekeeping, a banking word for a deposit. Jesus used it for His own spirit in Luke 23:46, and Paul used it of the elders and churches in Acts 14:23. Giving the church over to God is like leaving a deposit with someone who cannot lose it. Finally, 'I did not shrink back' in verses 20 and 27 is hypostello, a verb that also describes drawing back out of fear. Hebrews 10:38 uses it of the one who draws back and takes no pleasure in God. Paul's shepherding is the opposite of timid withdrawal.

The saying of Jesus in verse 35 is the one place where the New Testament preserves a word of the Lord that none of the four Gospels records. Luke gives it as something Paul 'remembered' (mnemoneuo), which suggests it circulated in the early church as a treasured word.

typology.type: The farewell charge: Moses, Joshua and Samuel
typology.fulfillment: Moses spoke to Israel before he died and handed over to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31), Joshua gathered the tribes to warn them before his own end (Joshua 23 and 24), and Samuel asked Israel to bear witness that he had taken nothing from anyone (1 Samuel 12:3-5). Paul does all three in one speech: he hands the flock on, warns of what will come, and says he coveted no one's silver or gold (20:33). The pattern is a leader who ends his work by saying his hands are clean. The fulfilment in Christ is that the Lord does not hand over a flock to a successor and leave. He promises to be with His people to the end of the age. The type falls short because Moses and Joshua could only warn; the gospel gives the Spirit to build up what they could only describe.

typology.type: The shepherds and the wolves, verses 28 to 29
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel 34 condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves, and the LORD promises to become the shepherd of His people. Paul places the elders in the shepherd's role and names the threat as savage wolves, the same animal Jesus uses in John 10:12. The escalation is that the Shepherd has now come. Jesus is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11-15, and the Chief Shepherd to whom elders answer, 1 Peter 5:4. Human shepherds are therefore under-shepherds who care for a flock that is not theirs. The type falls short at one point: earthly shepherds protect sheep at the risk of their lives, but only Christ pays with His own life in the sheep's place.

typology.type: Eutychus and the prophets who raised the dead
typology.fulfillment: Elijah lay on the widow's son three times and cried to the LORD (1 Kings 17:21-22), and Elisha stretched himself on the Shunammite's boy (2 Kings 4:34-35). Paul throws himself on Eutychus and embraces him, then says his life is in him. The correspondence is deliberate and shows that the God of the prophets works through His apostles. The escalation is that the apostle acts in the name of the risen Jesus, who raised the widow's son at Nain and said He is the resurrection and the life. Eutychus is raised to live out ordinary years, while Christ's resurrection is the first of a new creation. The type falls short because Eutychus will die again.

Paul's wish to finish his course and complete the ministry he received from the Lord Jesus (20:24) matches the way the Lord Jesus set His face toward Jerusalem. The correspondence is of path and attitude, not of work: Paul goes toward chains, as his Lord went toward the cross. The escalation is that Christ's journey accomplished something Paul's cannot, the atoning work that purchased the church (20:28). Paul's course is to testify to that finished work. The type falls short at the point of merit. Paul's life is offered, as 2 Timothy 4:6 says, like a drink offering poured out, but it does not buy anyone's pardon; only the blood of verse 28 does that.

study.christ:
The summit of the chapter is verse 28, and it is entirely about Christ's work. The church belongs to God because God acquired it, and the price was blood. Everything in the elders' work flows from that fact. They are not building their own institution or recruiting their own following. They are looking after what was bought at a cost they can never repay. Other New Testament texts fill in the claim. Ephesians 1:7 says that in Christ we have redemption through His blood, and Romans 3:25 speaks of the atoning sacrifice in His blood. Paul has said in one breath what he says at length in his letters.

The chapter also leads to Christ by the figure of the shepherd. John 10:11 gives the Lord's own claim: 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.' The elders are called to shepherd the flock, but they are always under-shepherds of someone else's sheep, and the contrast Jesus draws with the hired hand who runs from the wolf sets the standard. 1 Peter 5:4 gives the same picture from the other side: the Chief Shepherd will appear and reward faithful elders. Paul's warning about wolves is thus a call to be, in a small way, like the Shepherd who stood between the wolf and the flock.

Christ is also present in the quotation that closes the speech. 'It is more blessed to give than to receive' is attributed to the Lord Jesus Himself, and it summarises His own life, for He came not to be served but to give His life as a ransom. Paul's example of working with his own hands is therefore an imitation of Christ's own self-giving and not a quirk of personality.

There is a quieter link in the scene at Troas. The meeting is described as a gathering to break bread on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection. Whatever one decides about the nature of that meal, the church's weekly rhythm is already built around the risen Lord, and the story of the young man who is given back alive on that very day is a small sign pointing to the greater one. We should not press this further than the text, since Luke does not call Eutychus a type of Christ, but the placement is hard to miss.

Finally, verse 24 shows what it looks like to be held by Christ: Paul counts his life of no value if he can only finish the ministry he received from the Lord Jesus. The Lord who gave the ministry is the same Lord whose blood bought the flock. The speech begins and ends in Him.
study.god:
The speech shows the three persons of the Godhead at work in the life of a church, without once using that vocabulary. The Spirit presses Paul on, speaks in every city, and appoints the elders to their watch. God the Father is the owner of the church and the one who acquired it, and He is the one to whom the elders are commended (20:32). The Lord Jesus is the source of Paul's ministry (20:24), the author of the saying about giving (20:35), and the One whose blood paid the price. A pastor who asks where authority in the church comes from is meant to look here: the Spirit appoints, the Father owns, and the Son has paid.

The God of this passage is also a God who gives away what He values most. He did not purchase the church cheaply, and then entrust it to a man who might fail it. He commits it to the word of His grace, which Paul says can build the elders up and give them an inheritance. The elders are weak and the wolves are strong, but the keeping of the church does not depend on the elders' strength. This holds together two truths that are easy to separate: the elders must keep watch, and God keeps the church. Paul warns them night and day with tears, and then leaves them in God's hands, and sees no contradiction.

There is a quiet note about God's relationship to suffering. The Spirit warns of chains and does not remove them. Paul says that he is compelled by the Spirit and does not know what will happen, and yet he does know that chains await him. God's guidance in this passage is not a map of the future but a person to walk with. The elders weep, and no one tells them that the sorrow is misplaced.

For worship, the passage teaches that grief and praise belong together. Verse 36 says that Paul knelt down with them all and prayed, and the weeping and embracing that follow are not weakness. A church that has been shepherded well mourns when its shepherd goes, and it commits him to the same God to whom he committed them. The only response that fits a church bought with blood is wholehearted service of the One who paid.

crossReferences.note: Peter gives the elders the same charge in nearly the same words: shepherd God's flock, not by compulsion or for gain, but as examples, and look for the Chief Shepherd's reward. Seeing the two texts together shows that this was not a private preference of Paul's but the shared teaching of the apostles.

Jesus is the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, in contrast to the hired hand who runs from the wolf. Paul's wolves in verse 29 are the same enemy, and the price named in verse 28 is the laying down of life that Jesus describes here.

God condemns the shepherds who feed themselves and neglect the flock, and promises to search for His sheep Himself. Paul's insistence that the church belongs to God, and that he took nothing from them, takes its meaning from this chapter.

The character list for an overseer, written to Timothy in this same city. It shows what kind of person the Spirit makes an overseer: above reproach, able to teach, not greedy. Paul's own example at Miletus, working with his hands and coveting no one's gold, is the pattern behind the list.

Paul tells Titus to appoint elders in every town and then, in the next breath, describes the overseer. The easy slide from one word to the other is the best evidence outside Acts 20 that the two terms name the same office.

The watchman who warns is free of the blood of those who ignore him, and the watchman who stays silent is held accountable. Paul's claim in 20:26 that he is innocent of the blood of all men, because he did not shrink back from declaring the whole will of God, is this passage applied to preaching.

Paul's last letter echoes the farewell at Miletus. He is being poured out like a drink offering, and he has finished the race, using the same word for the course as in Acts 20:24. What he said he hoped to do, he has now done.

Elijah stretches himself over the widow's son and the child's life returns to him. Luke's account of Paul and Eutychus recalls the scene, and the words 'his life is in him' echo the language of the child's life returning, placing Paul in the line of the prophets.

Jesus warns of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are ravenous wolves inside. Paul's wolves in 20:29 are outsiders, and his further warning in verse 30 that some will come from within the elders themselves reflects the disguise Jesus describes.

Leaders keep watch over the souls of the flock as those who must give an account. The sentence looks at the same relationship from the other direction: the elders at Miletus are told to watch, and the congregation is told to let them do it with joy and not with grief.

Believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit as the pledge of the inheritance, until the redemption of those who are God's possession. The language of possession and inheritance matches Paul's words to the elders in 20:28 and 20:32, written to the same church in a calmer season.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden and a command to keep it, and it keeps returning to the question of who looks after God's people. Adam failed to guard the garden when the serpent came. Israel's kings and priests failed the flock, and Ezekiel 34 is the record of that failure along with God's promise to shepherd His sheep Himself. The prophets looked for a shepherd from David's line. Jesus claims that role in John 10, and He is the one who lays down His life. The farewell at Miletus belongs at the point where the Chief Shepherd has risen and returned to the Father, and the flock is handed to under-shepherds appointed by His Spirit.

The chapter also answers what happens to a mission when its founder leaves. The story of Acts has so far been told through Peter, Stephen, Philip, Barnabas and above all Paul. Here Paul says that none of the elders will see his face again. The answer is that the church does not rest on the founder. It rests on God, on the word of His grace, and on the shepherds the Spirit raises up. The command to watch for wolves is the practical form of that answer, and later chapters, and the letters to Timothy and to the churches of Asia, show how well it was needed.

Another thread is the purchase. In the Old Testament God acquires a people at the Red Sea, calling them His own possession (Exodus 15:16, Exodus 19:5). In Acts 20:28 the same idea is carried to its end: He acquired the church with blood. The story that began with one family becomes a people, and the people becomes a church that belongs to Him at a cost that cannot be undone.

The end of the story is the reunion Paul's friends wept over. The elders kissed him and grieved that they would never see his face again, and the New Testament answers that grief with the picture of the Chief Shepherd appearing, and of the crown of glory that does not fade, 1 Peter 5:4. In the new creation the Lamb at the centre of the throne will be the shepherd of His people and will lead them to springs of living water, and the farewells of the first century will be undone.

quiz.q: Why does Paul call the church so precious in verse 28?

options.text: Because God purchased it with His own blood.
options.note: Paul grounds the flock's worth in the price Christ paid, His own blood.

options.text: Because the Holy Spirit appointed overseers to lead it.
options.note: True and stated in the verse, but the reason for its preciousness is the purchasing blood, not the appointment of leaders.

options.text: Because Paul had labored among them for three years.
options.note: Paul's long labor is real, but the flock's value rests on Christ's purchase, not on Paul's effort.

options.text: Because the church in Ephesus was large and influential.
options.note: Its worth is not size or influence but the blood that bought it.

quiz.q: What do the words elder, overseer, and shepherd describe in this speech?

options.text: One office named three ways: standing, oversight, and shepherd care.
options.note: Paul calls the same men elders, says the Spirit made them overseers, and tells them to shepherd.

options.text: The same leaders, with shepherding as their main daily task.
options.note: Rightly sees them as the same men, but narrows the point; the terms together name one office in its full scope.

options.text: Three separate ranks of leadership in the church.
options.note: Later tradition distinguished ranks, but here the terms fall on the same men, not on a hierarchy.

options.text: Three unrelated groups who happened to gather at Miletus.
options.note: The text addresses one group, the Ephesian elders, throughout.

quiz.q: How does Paul say the elders should guard the flock?

options.text: By watching themselves and the flock, and resting the church on God and the word of His grace.
options.note: Paul charges self-watch first, then vigilance for the flock, and commits them to God and His grace.

options.text: By staying alert against wolves who come from outside the church.
options.note: True, but incomplete; Paul warns that some will rise from within their own number too.

options.text: By collecting silver and gold to fund the ministry.
options.note: Paul says the opposite, that he coveted no one's silver and worked with his hands.

options.text: By relying on Paul's ongoing presence to keep them safe.
options.note: Paul is leaving and commits them not to himself but to God and the word of His grace.

quiz.q: What compels Paul toward Jerusalem despite the warnings?

options.text: The Spirit compels him, and he counts his life of no value if he may finish his ministry.
options.note: Paul says he is bound in the Spirit and holds his life cheap to complete his course.

options.text: He wants to deliver the collection and see the church there.
options.note: True to his wider plans, but here he names the Spirit's compulsion and his resolve to finish the ministry.

options.text: He is confident nothing bad will happen to him there.
options.note: The reverse: the Spirit warns him city by city that chains and afflictions await.

options.text: He is fleeing the plot of the Jews in Greece.
options.note: The plot changed his route earlier, but it is not what drives him to Jerusalem.

quiz.q: What happened to Eutychus at Troas?

options.text: He fell from a window and died, and Paul restored him alive.
options.note: The young man was picked up dead, and Paul embraced him and declared him alive.

options.text: He fell asleep during the sermon and was gently woken.
options.note: He did sink into sleep, but the point is that he fell to his death and was raised.

options.text: He was injured in the fall but recovered on his own over time.
options.note: The text says he was taken up dead and then restored, not that he slowly recovered.

options.text: He was unharmed and simply went home early.
options.note: He fell from the third story and was picked up dead before being restored.

questions: Paul told the elders to keep watch over themselves first, and then the flock. Why does guarding your own soul have to come before caring for others, and how are you doing at it?
The church is precious because it was bought with Christ's own blood. How would seeing other believers as blood-bought change the way you treat them this week?
Paul warned that danger would come both from savage wolves outside and from men within their own number. Where do you see the church today needing that same alertness?
Paul committed the elders not to himself but to God and to the word of His grace. What are you tempted to lean on for security instead of God and His word?
Paul said it is more blessed to give than to receive and worked with his own hands to help the weak. Where is God calling you to give rather than to grasp?
The Ephesians wept most because they would not see Paul's face again, yet the mission went on. How does it comfort you that the church belongs to Christ and not to any one leader?

translationNotes.note: The church of God which He purchased with His own blood carries a footnoted alternative, with the blood of His own Son. Either way the flock is bought at the price of Christ's blood.
One Greek office is named by three words in this verse and its context: elder, overseer, and shepherd, describing the same men in their standing, their oversight, and their pastoral care.
